lesson.title: The Cigar Maker Who Defined American Unionism
lesson.summary: Samuel Gompers, an immigrant cigar maker from London, helped found and then led the American Federation of Labor for nearly four decades, shaping a cautious, practical brand of unionism that dominated organized labor into the twentieth century.
lesson.body:
Samuel Gompers was born in 1850 in London to a Jewish family and immigrated with them to New York City in 1863, while still a teenager. He learned the cigar making trade and joined the Cigar Makers International Union, an organization known for its tight discipline, regular dues, and strike funds, a model of steady, businesslike unionism that would deeply influence his later thinking.

Gompers helped found the American Federation of Labor in 1886 and was elected its first president. With the exception of a single year, 1895, when he was voted out and briefly replaced, he led the organization continuously until his death in December 1924, making him the dominant figure in American organized labor for nearly forty years.

Gompers's approach was famously pragmatic. He was known for boiling down organized labor's goals to a single idea: more, meaning steady, incremental gains in wages, hours, and working conditions rather than any grand ideological transformation of the economy. He was skeptical of socialism and of relying on government to solve labor's problems, preferring that unions win their gains directly from employers through organizing and bargaining. He also kept the AFL formally independent of any political party, a principle that distinguished his approach from labor movements in much of Europe.

Gompers's cautious, trade focused leadership helps explain why the AFL survived and grew where the Knights of Labor had collapsed, but it also carried forward the same limitations built into the AFL's structure: a labor movement centered on skilled, largely native born and white male trades, slower to embrace the millions of unskilled immigrant workers filling the nation's steel mills, mines, and railroads. Conflicts like the Homestead Strike and the Pullman Strike would soon reveal just how high the stakes of that gap could be.
